title: Ships loiter near subsea cables amid Iran's warnings to Trump
gist: Maritime intelligence firm Windward tracked three sanctioned Iran-linked tankers and a fishing boat loitering over Strait of Hormuz subsea cables in October, some going dark, as IRGC officials threaten cable attacks amid the US-Israel war with Iran. The war has already halted cable-ship operations, paused Meta-backed 2Africa expansion and accelerated bypass routes.

insights.claim: Windward tracked three sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing boat loitering near major undersea cables around the Strait of Hormuz in October, some switching off AIS transponders.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Precursor behavior to sabotage raises tail risk for Gulf connectivity and data-center operations.
insights.locator: The movements of three sanctioned tankers

insights.claim: Windward said the ship behavior suggests the vessels may be mapping cable routes or placing charges or mines on them while dark.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Signals elevated probability of a cable-cutting event, which would hit Gulf telecom and cloud services.
insights.quote: mapping the cable routes, or placing charges or mines on them while dark

insights.claim: Six active cables cross the Strait of Hormuz with two more under construction, and Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar depend entirely on these subsea links for outside connectivity.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Concentrated single-point-of-failure risk for Gulf economies' digital infrastructure.

insights.claim: One third of India's westbound Internet traffic goes through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Disruption would spill over to India's IT services and digital economy.
insights.quote: one third of India’s westbound Internet traffic goes through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz

insights.claim: An IRGC spokesperson on October 20 explicitly reminded the enemy that seven major cables run through the Strait of Hormuz, following Trump's threats to renew strikes.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Explicit state threat against digital infrastructure tied to escalation dynamics.
insights.quote: We remind the enemy of this.

themes.theme: War damage to Gulf tech infrastructure

insights.claim: Iran has launched multiple drone strikes on Amazon data centers in the Middle East and in May 2026 threatened to impose fees on Internet cables owned by US tech companies.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Physical risk to hyperscaler Gulf regions; may shift data-center investment away from the region.
insights.locator: Iran has also made a point

insights.claim: October marked the highest number of Iranian attacks on commercial ships since the war began in February 2026.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Escalating shipping attacks raise oil, freight and insurance risk premia.
insights.locator: The latest phase of the war

insights.claim: Cable-laying ships have been unable to safely enter the region since the war began, forcing the Meta-backed 2Africa cable to pause its planned expansion.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Repair capacity loss means any cut would take long to fix, amplifying outage duration.
insights.locator: Much damage has already been done

insights.claim: The war has compelled US tech companies and Gulf countries to accelerate alternative cable routes bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Capex tailwind for subsea cable builders and overland/alternative routes.
insights.locator: Much damage has already been done

insights.claim: Subsea infrastructure is increasingly at risk from sabotage and gray-zone warfare from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean, not just the Middle East.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Structural demand for cable resilience, monitoring and maritime surveillance services.
